NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: The other G2 and three lessons that follow for India
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
Few ideas cause greater anxiety in the Indian strategic community than a “G2”. It invokes fears of a US-China partnership that might produce geopolitical duopoly over Asia. But Delhi should also reflect on another G2 — a strategic accommodation between America and Russia. India has fewer reasons to fear it, although it would bring complications of its own.
US President Donald Trump ’s decision last week to ease sanctions on Russian diesel puts that possibility, distant though it might be, back in focus. After a telephone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin , Trump announced Russian supplies for American and global markets. Washington authorised diesel imports until April 2027. With diesel above $6 per gallon and the question of inflation hovering over congressional elections on November 3, cheaper fuel for farmers and truckers is an urgent political priority for Trump.
The irony is plain. Just weeks ago, Trump signed legislation giving him sweeping powers to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries like India buying Russian oil. Hypocritical? Of course. But hypocrisy is part of international life. For all the grandstanding on global issues by major powers, we know that all politics is local.
For Delhi, better US-Russia relations could reduce the friction that its Russian partnership creates with Washington. Many would hope that, having carved out an exemption on diesel for himself, Trump would hesitate to impose fresh oil sanctions on India. More interesting, though, is the prospect of an entente between Washington and Moscow that Trump has long championed.
Trump’s desire for better relations with Russia is hardly a secret. In his first term, he pressed for Moscow’s return to the G8, which suspended Russia after its annexation of Crimea in 2014. At Helsinki in 2018, he resisted calling Russia an adversary. He has repeatedly invoked the US-Soviet alliance in World War II as a sensible precedent for a new partnership.
But Trump’s first term also showed how difficult it is to build an internal American consensus on engagement with Russia. Democrats devoted considerable energy to portraying Trump as “Putin’s puppet” and arguing that Russian interference had helped put him in the White House. After taking the House in 2019, they pursued investigations into his Russian connections. If Democrats regain Congress, or even the House, they could use investigations, sanctions legislation and control over spending to obstruct a rapprochement with Moscow. Entrenched Republican opposition to concessions for Putin adds another constraint.
Some on America’s Christian right favour engagement with Putin, whom they see as a defender of traditional Western values against liberal cultural extremism. But that support cannot overcome the wider opposition.
Despite Washington’s well-known resistance to Russian engagement, Trump wasted no time in his second term pursuing better relations with Russia. Talks in Riyadh in February 2025 reopened high-level engagement. Putin’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, offered opportunities in energy, Arctic development and minerals. The Alaska summit that August brought the two presidents together but failed to end the war so far.
Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Putin in Moscow last month. Trump could meet Putin at November’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, where the Kremlin has floated a meeting including China’s Xi Jinping. He might also host Putin at December’s G20 summit in Miami. Moscow has yet to accept that invitation. Neither encounter is assured, but the diplomatic possibilities are expanding.
Commerce is central to Trump’s outreach to Russia. He wants economic cooperation to open a path to peace, rather than follow a settlement. Profitable ventures, he believes, can soften political antagonisms. American access to Russian energy and minerals could create a constituency for better relations. Trump also sees the Ukraine war as an obstacle to business and has pressed Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries.
Putin has reasons to bargain. Sanctions relief promises revenue, investment and technology. Engagement with Washington restores standing and could reduce dependence on China. A settlement recognising Russian territorial gains would let him claim victory at home. But translating these shared interests into concrete results has proved difficult. Ukraine will resist a bargain that rewards invasion or compromises its security. Just as Asian countries worry about a US-China compact, Europeans fear that a Trump-Putin bargain could leave them exposed to Russia’s geopolitical assertions.
Three lessons follow for India. First, US-Russia relations are not static. Their confrontation need not last forever. Delhi should consider the opportunities from US-Russian cooperation as carefully as the costs of hostility. A thaw could ease American pressure on India’s Russian energy purchases and defence ties.
Second, Moscow does not see confrontation with America as a “sacred ideological obligation”, as some in Delhi might believe. Russia values engagement with America as a great-power peer, even if it is no economic equal. In the early 1990s, Russia’s eagerness to build relations with America pushed India down Moscow’s priorities. Delhi should remember that experience.
Third, India’s stakes in Europe have risen dramatically. Trade, technology, investment and defence give Delhi a direct interest in European stability. Even if Trump and Putin strike a deal, Russia’s confrontation with Europe could continue. An American-Russian accommodation would therefore meet only part of India’s needs.
Delhi should contribute wherever it can to peace in Ukraine. It should also encourage direct dialogue between Russia and Europe on ending the war in Ukraine and shaping a sustainable security order in Europe and more broadly in Eurasia.
The writer is a contributing editor on international affairs for The Indian Express. He is professor and director at the Motwani Jadeja Institute of American Studies, Jindal Global University, Delhi

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: ‘Forced minor to drink chicken blood, raped believer’: Karnataka exorcist arrested
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
The Karnataka Police Monday arrested a self-proclaimed exorcist accused of repeatedly raping a woman under the pretext of driving out an evil spirit. While Satish Patri remained elusive for nearly a month, investigations revealed that a police constable helped him evade arrest by leaking police movements.
Patri, a well-known practitioner of black magic in Chikkamagaluru and neighbouring districts, was apprehended from a house in Bengaluru ’s J P Nagar and remanded to judicial custody.
The Chikkamagaluru district police registered two separate cases against Patri under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, and the Karnataka Prevention and Eradication of Inhuman Evil Practices and Black Magic Act.
In the first case, registered on August 23, a complainant alleged that Patri, who worked as the chief priest at a temple and carried out exorcisms for nearly five years, extorted money primarily from women. The complainant said that Patri threatened women with dire consequences and black magic if they failed to appear before him when summoned.
When Naik and local villagers questioned Patri on August 20, the accused allegedly abused them and issued death threats. Though Patri initially secured bail in this case, public anger mounted as videos circulated online showing him abusing women, extorting money, and allegedly forcing a minor girl to drink chicken blood in the name of exorcism.
Following the viral videos, a woman from Hassan approached the police on September 3, alleging that Patri had exploited her superstitious beliefs and repeatedly raped her near a temple since 2023. Meanwhile, the first complainant filed an application to cancel Patri’s bail, but a local court rejected it. An appeal remains pending before the Karnataka High Court.
Constable suspended
Patri went into hiding after his bail was cancelled. To avoid detection, he allegedly refrained from using SIM cards or standard calls, communicating solely through internet data and conference calls on a new mobile phone.
Multiple police teams were formed to track him down, and investigators discovered that a constable, identified as Kantesh, was tipping off the accused about police moves. The Chikkamagaluru district police subsequently suspended Kantesh for misconduct.
The police suspect many more victims exist who have not yet come forward.
“During our investigation, we found that a lot of women had undergone such trauma but are hesitant to file complaints due to fear,” a police officer said. “Even the victim in our case had been suffering since 2023, but only filed the complaint after the first case was registered and the videos went viral.”

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Sambhal police prevent minor’s marriage to 50-year-old man
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
An alert from child protection groups led Sambhal police to prevent the alleged marriage of a 16-year-old girl to a 50-year-old man in the Nakhasa police station area. The marriage was scheduled for Thursday, and the girl’s parents had allegedly agreed to it in exchange for Rs 5 lakh.
Station Officer Sanjay Kumar told The Indian Express that the local child protection organisation Prayatna alerted police on Tuesday evening about a minor being forced to marry an older man. A police team reached the house, which belonged to the alleged middleman, and found the girl there. Her parents and the middleman had fled, Kumar said.
The girl was taken to a One-Stop Centre before being placed in the care of the district Child Welfare Committee (CWC) on Wednesday. After the marriage was stopped, the CWC handed her back to her parents after obtaining an undertaking that any further attempt to arrange such a marriage would invite legal action, Kumar said.
In her statement to police, the girl said her family had taken her to the house on the pretext of attending a ceremony. She learnt that her marriage was being arranged only after reaching the venue, where preparations were already underway. She told police that the haldi ceremony was scheduled for Wednesday and the wedding procession for Thursday.
The girl said her parents were farm labourers and the family was poor. She is the eldest of five siblings — three girls and two boys. None of the children attends school, she told police.
Prayatna had received the alert from Just Rights for Children (JRC), an organisation working on child protection. Jitendra Parmar of JRC told The Indian Express that a local resident had informed the organisation about the proposed marriage between the minor and a 50-year-old widower.
According to Parmar, police and volunteers found that the rituals were already underway when they reached the house. While the girl’s parents and the middleman had fled, the middleman’s wife and children were present with the girl.
Police have recorded the rescue in their station records, Kumar said.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Why Emirates is averse to shifting some flights to Navi Mumbai airport
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
Dubai-based mega airline Emirates would prefer to keep its existing flight operations in Mumbai at the Mumbai airport rather than shifting some of the flights from there to the Navi Mumbai airport located about 50 km away, according to a senior airline official who said that the new airport is not ready yet for large-scale international operations by global airlines. The comments from Emirates — the largest overseas carrier operating to and from India — come at a time when the Adani group, which operates both Mumbai and Navi Mumbai airports, wants a third of international flights at the former to shift to the new greenfield airport.
“(The Navi Mumbai ) Airport is not ready…At an airport you would require facilities for catering, you would require a facility, for example, for cargo warehousing. So those elements, until it gets kind of fully built into an ecosystem, I think it’s going to be difficult for any of the airlines to shift,” said Essa Sulaiman Ahmad, Emirates’s senior vice president of commercial operations for West Asia and Indian Ocean. Ahmad was speaking with reporters at an event to mark the launch of the airline’s Airbus A380 service to and from Delhi.
Some time back, the Adani group-controlled Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL) had informed airlines that it would reduce 265 international flights per week — from a total of 770 international weekly flights — from October 25 as it planned to start work on revamping the older passenger terminal at the Mumbai airport. The airport operator had asked the airlines to move a third of their flights to Navi Mumbai, or suspend those flights till the renovation work is completed, which is likely to take about four years. As per Mumbai airport’s calculations, Emirates would have had to shift 10 of its weekly flights from Mumbai airport.
Following pushback from carriers and intervention by the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA), it has now been decided that no international flight will be shifted out of Mumbai airport at least till March-end . In the interim, the airport operator and the airlines will work jointly to develop a plan to manage the capacity issue from next year’s summer schedule.
According to Ahmad, Emirates would consider newer Indian airports, including Navi Mumbai, if the India-Dubai bilateral air services agreement is expanded to have more seat capacity entitlements — something the airline and Dubai have been seeking from India for years now. But as far as the current scale of operations go, the airline is happy operating from its existing bases in India. Emirates currently has 167 weekly flights from nine Indian cities, including 35 from Mumbai and 28 from Delhi.
“I think for us it’s plain and simple. We’ve been having our operations in Mumbai airport for a very long time. We do not have (scope for) additional flights as part of our air services agreements and entitlements to operate into any new airport or any new destination…(if) we get additional seat entitlements, then we will definitely look at multiple new (Indian) airports that have come,” Ahmad said.
If that indeed happens, Emirates would actively evaluate Navi Mumbai, Ahmad said, noting that it represents an attractive new market, as it is closer to Pune than the Mumbai airport, and also offers better and faster connectivity to the Nhava Sheva Port and some other commercial areas.
The India-Dubai air services agreement allows a total of about 66,000 seats per week per direction for the Indian as well as Dubai-based airlines. The quota was fully exhausted by both sides a few years ago. Dubai has been seeking an expansion of the bilateral flying rights, but India has been reluctant to do so.
The Indian government and major Indian carriers like Air India and IndiGo have ambitions to have more direct international connectivity from India. A significant number of passengers flying to far-off destinations from India take connecting flights through major global hubs outside the country, Dubai and Doha for instance. India wants its carriers to ramp up wide-body operations, instead of facilitating foreign airlines, particularly Gulf-based carriers with deep pockets, in ferrying passengers to Europe and beyond through their massive hub airports.

I know that there are 100 different things you can do, but I tried and tested, and this is something I follow, and it is non-negotiable wherever I am and however busy I am. While mentioning people’s contentions and doubts, she shared her experiences and how it has helped her. “I know, people sometimes frown on that, but when I was going through a particularly difficult period, I was told to write this gratitude journal . For the first few months, I found it excruciatingly hard to write positive things in this journal, especially because I wasn’t feeling that way. From a psychological perspective, gratitude journaling can be a useful tool for directing attention towards positive or meaningful aspects of everyday life. At the same time, mental health advocates and psychotherapists like Delnna Rrajesh note that gratitude should not become another obligation to feel positive. “When someone is struggling, forcing themselves to write happy thoughts can feel unnatural or even frustrating. A more practical approach is to acknowledge what they are genuinely experiencing while identifying small things they appreciate, such as a supportive person, a comforting meal, or simply getting through a difficult day.”

Consultant dietitian and fitness expert Garima Goyal noted that morning light also has a physiological role. “Exposure to natural light after waking helps regulate the body’s circadian rhythm, supporting the sleep-wake cycle and alertness during the day. Spending some time outdoors in the morning, while following sensible sun-protection practices, can be a simple addition to a daily routine ,” said Goyal.
The broader lesson is that a morning routine need not involve dozens of habits or an elaborate wellness checklist. “A few consistent practices that support mental clarity, movement, light exposure and emotional well-being may be more realistic and sustainable than trying to follow every new health trend,” Goyal told indianexpress.com .
A good routine doesn’t force positivity every day; it creates space to respond to life with greater awareness and resilience.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Working to develop ties with China, last word not yet scripted: Piyush Goyal
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
In remarks reflecting Delhi’s calibrated economic and diplomatic engagement with Beijing despite tensions along the frontier, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said Wednesday that India is working to “develop” its relations with China, but the last word on this journey has “not yet been scripted”.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar flagged concerns over economic issues with China, underlining the “one-sided” and “tilted” trade balance.
On India’s ties with the US, Jaishankar said the two two countries continue to engage to iron out differences over the proposed bilateral trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a “landing point”.
Goyal said India-US relations are “very good” and will only improve irrespective of changes in political thinking in the two countries.
The two ministers were speaking at different panel discussions at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
On China, Goyal said, “We are open to all countries around the world as long as we get a fair deal, as long as we ensure a continuity in the engagement, and as long as the geopolitical situation does not deteriorate. I think we had some concerns in the past. We are working to develop relations with China once again, but the last word has not yet been scripted on this journey.”
Jaishankar said, “We also have very major economic issues with China. If you look today at the trade balance, it is completely tilted (towards China).”
“The tilt is extremely one-sided, and in many sectors where we have done well with the rest of the world, we have not had market access. We have not had a successful business operation for that sector in China,” he said.
“We do believe today that we are not getting a level playing field in China in the manner in which we have given a level playing field to them,” he said.
Ties between India and China have been strained for the last six years due to the military standoff along the Line of Actual Control. But the two countries have been making efforts to repair ties following the rapprochement in the last two years and also because of the economic imperatives due to US tariffs. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi last month.
On India-US ties, Jaishankar said the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.
On Tuesday, responding to a question on the trade negotiations, he said, “I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn’t be comfortable spilling the beans in public.”
He said Goyal and the US Trade Representative (USTR) and other officials concerned have been engaged in talks to move forward on the bilateral trade pact.
“When countries negotiate with an economy like the United States, obviously one part of it is what you work out between yourselves and the US, and one part of it is how do you fare vis-a-vis competitive economies. And that part of it is not entirely clear because not everybody has worked out a deal. I think people, the trade ministers, USTR there and our Commerce and Industry Minister are there, working on that. They are ironing it out. My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point,” he said.
Jaishankar also outlined Washington’s new approach on economic engagement. “The US has a fundamentally different approach to the use of tariffs. But even that is a symptom of something else. The US is today determined to re-industrialise and to reset the terms of access to its economy,” he said.
“That’s what the whole tariff debate is about. And the two are connected: access to the American economy and the re-industrialisation of America. Therefore, what is happening is every significant economy is getting into a negotiation with the United States on this issue. We are not alone in this. In our case, we are pretty far advanced in that process of negotiation,” he said.
Jaishankar also said that the US is revising the terms of its alliances and treaty relationships, and that the sentiment is most strongly being felt in Europe, and to some extent, in some countries in East Asia.
“We have many issues we are working on with the United States, but we don’t have an issue of the terms of alliance because we are not officially an ally. We are a country which has a strong strategic partnership with the US, but a strategic partnership is a partnership. It’s not an alliance,” he said.
“In our case, for the last 20-odd years, we have worked out what we felt were convergences, overlaps, shared common interests with the US, and we had agreed that we would pursue that. I don’t think that has fundamentally changed,” he said.
Goyal said the India-US bilateral relationship goes beyond trade and encompasses defence, technology, critical minerals and people-to-people ties.
“Of course, it is already very good. I don’t see any problem as we speak. And to my mind, the relationship with the US that India enjoys is very substantive, very consequential for the world, being two large democracies,” he said, responding to a question on whether bilateral ties would improve once US President Donald Trump leaves office.
“It’s not only about trade… They are our largest trading partner and, I think, will continue to be in the years to come. And by and large, I don’t see any problem in any agreements also with the United States,” he said.
“It’s about trade, it’s about defence partnership, it’s our technology partnership, it’s our critical minerals partnership, it’s our people-to-people engagement,” he said.
“The US and India have a very, very consequential relationship and it’s only going to get better irrespective of changes in political thinking, whether in India or in the US. The relationship draws its strength from our economic imperatives, from our political imperatives, from our security imperatives. So it’s a very safe relationship. I don’t think the rest of the world needs to worry about it,” Goyal said.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Cheruvayal Raman, ‘father of rice’ who kept indigenous varieties alive, dies at 76
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
For most of his life, Cheruvayal Raman fought to preserve indigenous rice varieties, earning him the moniker ‘Nella achaan (father of rice)’ and a Padma Shri in 2023. On Wednesday, that battle came to an end — the tribal farmer breathed his last at the age of 76.
Raman was undergoing treatment at Kozhikode Medical College and Hospital.
A member of the Kurichiya tribe, Raman began working in paddy fields at the age of 10. Although he studied only up to Class 5, his knowledge of traditional rice cultivation and seed conservation made him a textbook model for agricultural scientists, farmers and researchers.
His journey into seed conservation began around 2000, when, inspired by agricultural enthusiasts who wanted him to preserve the seeds, he began collecting indigenous varieties from paddy fields across Wayanad and cultivating 4-5 rice varieties. Over the years, that collection grew to 55 kinds — many of them varieties he believed had all but vanished as traditional cultivation dwindled.
At a time when agricultural scientists and governments were promoting high-yielding hybrid seeds, Raman chose to preserve traditional varieties, despite their comparatively low yields and associated financial losses. But his task was tall, and critics of the “unprofitable pursuit” were plenty — some from his own family.
Between harvests, Raman would visit the paddy fields of Wayanad in search of different rice varieties. His rice bank slowly grew with every year, and by 2016, Raman cultivated all 55 varieties every year on his three acres of paddy land, dividing the fields into small plots to accommodate each variety. He did not sell the seeds but shared them with farmers on the condition that they return a portion of their harvest as seeds to sustain the practice.
“Farmers, one after another, have been abandoning paddy cultivation. Some of these seeds would have become history, but for my initiative. Nobody wants to follow this unattractive, loss-making cultivation of rice,” he said then.
Until the end, his search for new varieties and efforts to conserve them continued. He typically stored the seeds in bamboo baskets inside the century-old ancestral mud house he shared with his wife, Geetha, and his family. Despite receiving recognition from agricultural institutions and the government, he did not seek assistance to maintain his collection. His work also took him beyond India: in 2018, he presented his rice conservation mission at an international symposium in Brazil. He also received the National Plant Genome Saviour Award instituted by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Authority.
But despite the renown, he lived in his thatched straw-and-bamboo three-roomed house, with one narrow walkway. When he was honoured with the Padma Shri in the category of agriculture in 2023, Raman, a Class 5 dropout, told The Indian Express of the pressure of moving against the tide.
“They told me that I have become mad over rice. But I stuck by my decision, and now everyone has acknowledged it,” he said then.
In his condolence message, Keralam Chief Minister V D Satheesan called Raman a guardian and gene bank of rare paddy varieties. “Homage to the memory of this noble soul who truly understood soil, cherished the seeds, and lived for nature,” he said on X.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi also expressed his condolences. “Deeply saddened by the passing of Padma Shri Cheruvayal Raman, our beloved Ramettan. He devoted his life to preserving Wayanad’s indigenous paddy seeds, keeping generations of Adivasi knowledge alive. I join the people of Wayanad in mourning him,” he wrote on X.
A post from his sister, Wayanad MP Priyanka Gandhi, was touching. In her long post on X, she wrote: “Cheruvayal Raman called me his daughter when I met him, and he touched my heart. From then on, I teased him and called him my Malayali Acchan. When we last spoke to each other a month back, he wanted me to go and meet him. I promised that I would, but I had to cut short my trip to Wayanad because of events in Delhi so I missed meeting him thinking that I would return soon.”
She added: “When I heard about his passing today, my heart sank. My Malayali acchan was wise, dignified and bold in thought and action. He wanted more for his people, he refused to accept less. His mind could not tolerate discrimination and injustice. He showed me his awards and honours with sadness in his eyes — he said they would mean nothing to him until his people could live better lives. He was a genius in his knowledge of paddy and agriculture and he understood the great value of his own culture and tradition. He was proud of his heritage and lived it with every breath. I will miss my wise friend and keep his teachings in my heart for always. India has lost a noble son.”

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Yogendra Yadav writes: Going forward, all protests must be one, coordinate efforts and energies
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
What next? What should we expect now in the medley of protests? Sitting in Bengali Market, I munched over this question, a good distraction from the chhole bhature that did not live up to their fame.
It was a good moment to ask this question. Monday, October 12, was the death anniversary of Rammanohar Lohia , who famously said “ zinda kaumein paanch saal tak intezar nahin karti ” (A living people do not wait for five years). Over the previous 10 days, I had been detained five times — grabbed, dragged, pushed and shoved into police vans — for peacefully protesting against the Chief Election Commissioner. This was one of those lucky days when I did not end up in a police station.
We had just returned from the march to the Supreme Court. This was not a protest against the judiciary, least of all an attempt to put pressure on the courts. If anything, it was to restore the majesty of the Supreme Court that lay tattered on the streets of Delhi this weekend. Above all, it was to assert our fundamental right to peaceful protest in the national capital that was placed under a virtual curfew and experienced a reign of terror in miniature. We had reclaimed the streets.
What should be the next move? Obviously, the movement has to be expanded both in geographical and social terms. Some new forms of action need to be devised, besides a routine of street demonstrations. Some new institutional pressure points need to be identified. While the strategy and tactics of the protest are being worked out, an understanding of the destination and route might help navigation.
Suhas Palshikar characterises the present protests as a moment of “redemocratisation”, as the way of opening the multiple systemic “closures” that we have witnessed (‘ Crackdown on Jantar Mantar 2.0, amid other closures, calls for redemocratisation ’, IE, October 13). These “closures” are a consequence of what I have called “democracy capture” that began in 2014 — a capture of democracy by using seemingly democratic means. The key instrument was “election capture”: Elections are held regularly, but the playing field is tilted progressively to insulate the regime from electoral defeat. It began with the taming of mass media and monopoly over money power, was supplemented by the capture of the Election Commission and misuse of the CBI and ED, and is finally taking the shape of permanent architectural changes by way of the SIR, delimitation and One-Nation-One-Election. The current protests are against this design to ensure a permanent majority for the BJP.
The protests are about restoration of electoral integrity. No more. No less. Although there is no official charter, three demands are shared by all the protesters. First, the resignation or impeachment of CEC Gyanesh Kumar , a symbolic act towards restoring the proper functioning and credibility of the ECI. Second, the rollback of the SIR, so as to undo the largest ever disenfranchisement in the history of democracy. Third, the repeal of the 2023 Act, which grants the regime unfettered powers to appoint anyone to the ECI and complete immunity to those appointed. The basic impulse underlying these demands is the quest for free and fair elections, at least as free and as fair as the election that brought the BJP to power in 2014. Nothing less would do.
At the same time, this protest is not about regime change. Many of the forces behind the protest may wish to see an exit for Prime Minister Narendra Modi, sooner rather than later. But this is not the sentiment that drives ordinary citizens to the streets. Not yet. As of now, it is about restoring a system that keeps open a fair possibility of a democratic and peaceful transfer of power. If this bare minimum demand is frustrated, and every legitimate avenue for redress remains closed, the present protest may morph into a popular upsurge for regime change. The human and systemic costs of that kind of upheaval would be terrifying. Thankfully, we are not there yet. We should continue to hope that the residual capacity of regulatory institutions and the sheer long-term self interest of the ruling party would prevent such a catastrophe. Popular mobilisation on the streets does not bypass the constitutional order. It generates countervailing pressure that can strengthen institutions against the overwhelming power exerted by the regime.
Steering the protests towards this objective would require a realignment of forces. So far, these protests are a textbook example of “spontaneous synchronisation”, where orderly collective action emerges without any central command or coordination. This happens when different actors, responding to one another, gradually align their actions without any conscious design or plan. The spontaneous call by “concerned citizens” (including this writer) leading to street action on October 2 to 4, the October 10 protest originally called by the CJP and the series of actions by the INDIA coalition from October 6 to 12 were not coordinated decisions. But the outcome appears like an orchestra or a relay race where the baton keeps changing hands.
That cannot be the way forward. If the regime has decided not to yield an inch, the protesters have to find a mechanism to coordinate their efforts. The CJP, the INDIA bloc, youth organisations and civil society may not and need not come under one umbrella, but they must ensure that they do not work at cross-purposes, that their energies cannot be deflected against one another. Fortunately, Rahul Gandhi has opened a window in this respect by stating that there are no separate or parallel protests, that all protests are one. Also, the relative strength of different strands of this movement has undergone a shift this time. This makes a realignment possible. The success of this movement hinges on this. The strength of organic or self-mobilised protesters, who were the backbone of the July youth protests, is critical here. These young protesters are not wedded to any organisation and their enthusiasm could be dampened if they find conflicting signals. Instead of an organisation- or party-led movement, they would like to see a citizens’ movement supported by parties and organisations.
My train of thought stopped here as the insipid “machine coffee” I was sipping got over. I resolved not to order anything except South Indian filter coffee. And not to take chhutti till Gyanesh Kumar gets his chhutti from the Election Commission.
The writer is member, Swaraj India, and national convenor, Bharat Jodo Abhiyan

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Where is the money going? Unpacking a decade of India’s private sector-led development
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
India has quietly created one of the world’s largest pools of private sector-led development finance through its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) law. What began as corporate compliance legislation in 2014, where companies crossing any of the three thresholds — Rs 500 crore in net worth, Rs 1,000 crore in turnover or Rs 5 crore in net profit — are mandated to spend 2 per cent of their net profits on CSR, has mobilised Rs 2.6 lakh crore in 10 years.
Recent reports indicate the annual CSR spend of Rs 40,794 cr in 2024-25, contributed by 29,500 companies supporting 72,000 projects. This is perhaps the world’s largest example of mandatory private-sector contribution.
India Inc. deserves credit. This is no longer charity at the margins of corporate balance sheets. It is a significant source of crucial development capital. The success of the CSR experiment in mobilising money must now evolve to maximising impact across the country and sectors.
The latest numbers show why: Maharashtra received Rs 8,631 crore, Gujarat Rs 4,549, Karnataka Rs 3,395 and Delhi Rs 2,753 crore of CSR funds last year. Together, these four states accounted for more than Rs 20,000 crore. Where companies are located can become a stronger determinant of CSR deployment than where India’s development deficits are greatest.
Optimising the impact of the CSR funds will be a crucial opportunity. The issue is not that CSR money is being poorly spent; much of it is extremely valuable in supporting education, health, and livelihoods. The larger question is what the thousands of individual projects are adding up to. As the CSR pool continues to grow, the opportunity is to optimise its strategic value. That requires greater attention to where the money goes and what outcomes they ultimately deliver. This points to three reforms for the next decade of CSR.
First, it is not just about the size of the cheque but also about the change it makes. The accountability framework that currently measures the amount spent will have to be combined with stronger outcome indicators and standardisation of what they measure.
Second, 72,000 projects provide enormous innovation and effort. But fragmented, often repetitive activities must turn into longer-term, strategic interventions. The CSR law already permits companies to collaborate. India Inc. should build on this by creating aggregations and combining funds and efforts around major themes and geographies. Ten companies investing Rs 10 crore individually on often unrelated, isolated projects may each produce useful outputs without changing the underlying system. Ten such companies coming together investing Rs 100 crore against a common results framework can potentially change a district system and have a much larger impact.
Third, CSR is likely to create greater impact when companies deploy not just their money, but also their knowledge, networks and managerial capabilities. An agriculture or food company, for example, may be better placed to support farmer productivity, value chains or climate-resilient agriculture than to fund an unrelated education programme. Aligning CSR more closely with a company’s core competency can make each rupee more strategic and scalable.
The real headline is not simply that Indian companies now spend over Rs 40,000 crore annually on CSR. It is what this capital could achieve to move national indicators — not as a substitute for public expenditure, but as a supplement to it. It also comes as a reminder that profit and purpose reinforce each other in creating value not only for the country but also for the companies that are standing by it.
The writer is a senior technology advisor. Views are personal

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: In Delhi protests, an erosion of liberty
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
Also by Ayan Aditya Giri
Every democracy, sooner or later, confronts the same difficult situation: A crowd on a public road, a police battalion, and a vehicle at the kerb. The mass detention of opposition leaders, students and other demonstrators in the ongoing protests in Delhi directed at the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, has brought that scene into Indian lives now. We do not weigh the protestors’ grievance, nor the necessity pleaded by the authorities. We ask the prior question: “What does the Constitution say about the street and about the detention cells?
Peaceful assembly is a settled commitment of constitutional democracies, but like other rights, it is never an absolute right. The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects the right to “peaceably assemble”. American courts permit reasonable regulation of time, place, and manner, yet since Brandenburg vs Ohio , they punish advocacy only when it is directed at, and likely to produce, imminent lawless action. Article 8 of the German Basic Law protects assembly “peacefully and without arms”. In the Brokdorf decision (1985), Germany’s Federal Constitutional Court treated demonstrations as integral to democratic order and required that restrictions be proportionate, with outright bans a “last resort”. Our Supreme Court, too, on October 9, clarified that only regulation, not prohibition, is permissible. Section 17 of the South African Constitution protects the right to demonstrate and picket “peacefully and unarmed”, and in Garvis (2012), the Constitutional Court tied the liability of organisers to what they could reasonably have prevented. Under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, 1950, as applied in DPP vs Ziegler (2021) by the UK Supreme Court, even disruptive protest demands a proportionality assessment.
The common thread is simple: Protest is presumptively protected; peacefulness is the condition of that protection.
The framers of India’s Constitution confronted the same tension, and many of them had been detained without trial themselves. Draft Article 15A, which became Article 22, was debated in September 1949. H V Kamath and Pandit Thakur Bhargava, among others, warned that a Constitution should not authorise detention on mere executive satisfaction. B R Ambedkar ’s answer was that a young state facing the violence of Partition could not be denied a power of preventive detention, but that the power should be hedged. The Assembly settled on safeguards: Grounds must be communicated, and detention beyond three months requires an Advisory Board’s approval. Preventive detention entered the Constitution as an acknowledged exception, not as an ordinary instrument of governance. Unfortunately, the 44th constitutional amendment of 1978 providing additional safeguards has not yet been notified.
The Supreme Court has since policed that exception. In Ram Manohar Lohia vs State of Bihar (1960), it held that even the detention on the call not to pay irrigation rates was illegal. In Ram Manohar Lohia (1966), the SC distinguished between “law and order”, “public order” and “security of the State” as three concentric circles, so that not every disturbance of peace justifies drastic measures. Only an aggravated situation of law and order can be termed as public order. The peaceful Delhi protests are at best a question of maintaining law and order. The way the police have treated MPs, lawyers and journalists despite the SC’s directions cannot be justified in the name of public order.
In Himat Lal K Shah (1973), the Court held the right to assemble peaceably to be fundamental yet regulable, but not subject to an official’s arbitrary refusal. Ramlila Maidan Incident, In re (2012) affirmed that peaceful protest cannot be extinguished by arbitrary executive action.
Justice D Y Chandrachud’s opinion in Arnab Goswami (2020) reminded us that even a day’s deprivation of liberty is a grave matter, while Justice H R Khanna’s dissent in ADM Jabalpur (1976) remains the standing answer to any suggestion that liberty rests on executive grace.
Ambedkar’s concluding speech to the Assembly on November 25, 1949, is salient in this regard. Where constitutional methods are open for achieving social and economic objectives, he said, there is no justification for unconstitutional ones, which he called the “grammar of anarchy”. He counted civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha among them. The same speech warned against hero-worship and against laying one’s liberties at the feet of even a great man. Read together, the two warnings impose reciprocal duties: Citizens must keep dissent peaceful and lawful, and the state must keep the constitutional avenues of dissent genuinely open.
In the light of this jurisprudence, three questions follow: Was the assembly peaceful? Was the apprehension of disorder specific and imminent rather than vague and general? And was the police response proportionate, with custody limited in duration, grounds communicated, and production before a magistrate within 24 hours as Article 22(1) and (2) require? Unlawful detention, even for an hour, is deprivation of one’s liberty. This right cannot be restricted to just one Arnab Goswami.
A democratic state shows its strength in tolerating the dissent it hears, and a democratic citizenry in keeping that dissent peaceful. Our Constitution asks both to remember that order and liberty are not rivals but co-tenants of one republic, and that each is safest when the other is respected.
Mustafa is a constitutional Law scholar, and Giri is a scholar at Chanakya National Law University, Patna. Views are personal

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: In Manipur, the work of peace is still to be done
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
Reports that at least nine people were killed in the latest outbreak of violence across Manipur’s hill districts on the night of October 9 point, yet again, to the state government’s incapacity to heal or contain schisms in the state. By all accounts, the violence between the Kuki and Naga communities spanned three districts — Kamjong, Kangpokpi and Senapati — and involved ambushes and gunfights by armed groups. It is disturbing that even after three-and-a-half years of ethnic violence, there is only a fragile calm, and little progress seems to have been made towards an enduring end to the conflict.
After the N Biren Singh government was dissolved in February 2025, it was hoped that President’s Rule would make space for an administration seen to be less partisan to stabilise the situation. But while large-scale violent clashes declined, normalcy remained elusive, and the deep divides that had taken hold since May 2023 persisted. As calls for an elected government grew louder, Yumnam Khemchand Singh, a Meitei like his predecessor, was chosen as chief minister. The appointment of a Kuki and a Naga deputy CM gave hope that political representation would pave the way for a lasting settlement. But the old Kuki-Naga fault line that fuelled bloodshed in the 1990s has been reopened. Since February, dozens of people from both communities have been killed and houses torched. The Meiteis, Kukis and Nagas are now caught in overlapping conflicts, with civilians bearing the brunt not only of the violence but also of blockades across the hill districts that restrict access to essential supplies.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi met CM Y Khemchand Singh on Saturday and promised all possible assistance to the embattled state government. But a return to normalcy will remain out of reach without a concerted effort, first, to demilitarise society and re-establish the state’s authority. In August, Singh issued a 15-day ultimatum for the voluntary surrender of illegal firearms, thousands of which have been looted from state armouries since the conflict began. This was not the first such appeal: Soon after President’s Rule was imposed in February 2025, Governor Ajay Kumar Bhalla had also called for the surrender of weapons. The continued prevalence of gun violence suggests that such appeals have not worked. Disarming armed groups and punishing those responsible for the killings must be an immediate priority. But the government must also create the conditions for sustained dialogue. Restoring the freedom of movement and making it possible for people to live safely alongside one another will have to be step one in a long process of reconciliation.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: As inflation inches upwards, can rate hike be far behind?
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
Retail inflation continues to inch upwards , rising to 5.54 per cent in September, up from 4.83 per cent in August, according to data from the National Statistics Office. With this print, inflation came in at 4.9 per cent in the second quarter, in line with the central bank’s most recent projection. Much of the increase in the headline inflation number is being driven by food prices. But price pressures are being felt in non-food categories as well. And with expectations of inflation firming up in the months ahead, it increases the odds of a tighter monetary policy.
Food inflation has surged to 7.74 per cent in September, up from 6 per cent in August, driven by items such as onions, ginger, garlic and lemon. The FAO food price index has also jumped 5.8 per cent, pointing towards an uptick in international prices. Weak rainfall will weigh heavily on output. The outlook remains uncertain. According to Crisil, “concerns over the rabi crop are also mounting amid low soil-moisture levels and elevated temperatures”. Early indicators for October point towards continuing price pressures. Rating agency ICRA expects food and beverage inflation to exceed 8 per cent in October. Alongside, global crude oil prices remain elevated. As on October 12, the price of the Indian crude oil basket was $125.7 per barrel. This will add to the pressures in the economy. Core inflation is also moving upwards to 4.3 per cent, which indicates the pass-through of higher costs. Higher food and cooking fuel prices have kept inflation in the restaurants and accommodation services category elevated.
Over the coming months, inflation is likely to rise further. Economists at SBI have projected CPI at 6.5 per cent in the third quarter and 5.6 per cent in the fourth quarter, while ICRA expects inflation at around 6 per cent in the third quarter. This raises the possibility of another rate hike when the RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee meets next, in the first week of December. While most expect the MPC to hike rates by 25 basis points, some suggest the likelihood of a 50 basis points hike. To what extent the committee tightens over the coming months will depend on its expectations of how inflation will evolve going forward.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: There are plenty more fish in the sea
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
If being omnivorous gave human beings an advantage in the high-stakes game of evolution, what is to be made of the growing evidence that the species’ palate has, in this age of plenty, narrowed rather than expanded? Consider, for example, the British palate, which according to research published this week in People and Nature, enjoys so little of what it once prized that fish and seafood consumption has effectively been reduced to a small group of fish. Gone are the plaice, herring and oysters, replaced almost entirely by the “Big Five”: Cod, haddock, salmon, prawns and tuna.
This is a paradox of the modern age, where a mindboggling diversity prevails everywhere, from fashion and pastimes to media and medicines, but the dinner plate — whether one is in New Delhi or New York — looks increasingly the same. There is of course, as there always is in the tangled web of the global economy, a range of reasons, including the dominance of monocultures. Humans now get the bulk of their calories from just eight crops: Rice, wheat, maize, potatoes, barley, palm oil, soy and sugar.
Beyond its implications for health — and there are many, given the ballooning global obesity crisis — the restricted diet of the contemporary human blunts the very evolutionary edge that helped ensure Homo sapiens’ success. The lessons are clear, especially in light of the monoculture-related food disasters of the modern age, such as the great banana epidemic that once wiped out entire plantations in South and Central America or the African swine fever that swept through Asia in 2018, leading to the culling of millions of pigs and disruption of the global food supply: There are plenty of fish in the sea, if only humans would pick a wider variety.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: FASTag at Delhi Airport: Can payment system be used to restrict entry?
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has taken cognisance of complaints regarding the use of FASTag for parking fee payments at the Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi.
Officials said that it was recently learnt that only vehicles with active FASTag were being allowed at the arrival lane of the Delhi airport’s Terminal 3 (or T3, which operates international and select domestic flights), while others were being diverted to the multi-level car parking (MLCP) facility located opposite the terminal. This results in many vehicles exhausting the free waiting time limit of 8 minutes.
We explain what the FASTag system is, the issue over using it to enforce entry restrictions, and how FASTag is used at the Delhi airport.
What is FASTag?
FASTag is an electronic toll collection system in India that NHAI operates using Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology for automatic and cashless toll payments directly from the customer’s linked savings or current account, or prepaid wallet.
An RFID tag has to be affixed to the vehicle’s windscreen, which scans automatically at toll plazas, deducting the fare directly from the linked account or wallet. If a FASTag is linked to a prepaid account, it needs to be recharged or topped up based on the customer’s usage. If the customer doesn’t maintain an adequate balance, the FASTag gets blacklisted.
FASTag is also vehicle-specific: once affixed to a vehicle, it cannot be transferred to another vehicle. It can be purchased from any of the National Electronic Toll Collection member banks — a group of over 40 financial institutions.
Apart from toll charges on the National Highways, FASTag is used for payment of parking fees in different parts of the cities as well.
What did officials say about usage of FASTag?
Officials said that FASTag is only a payment system and it cannot be used for enforcing the entry restrictions.
“It is about the purpose for which it is being used. FASTag is a payment instrument for parking facilities at airports and cannot be used as a means of enforcing entry restriction,” an official told The Indian Express .
“The matter has been taken cognisance of and the authority has directed the banks, which operate at the airport, to ensure that the system is only used for the payment and discontinue it from any such restriction,” the official added.
How is FASTag being used at the Delhi airport?
As things stand, the Delhi airport offers a free waiting time of 8 minutes for private vehicles in Lane 3 of T3’s arrivals area. This was introduced in October 2024 to reduce traffic congestion by ensuring a steady flow of vehicles in and out of the pickup lane. After 8 minutes, the airport charges Rs 250 for 9-13 minutes and Rs 500 for over 13 minutes of parking.
Making FASTag mandatory for entry into the arrival lane is inconvenient for many Delhi-NCR residents. According to the official, many vehicles don’t have an active FASTag or FASTag with sufficient balance since they do not need to use toll plazas for commuting within the city.
Many users on the social media platform X have shared their grievances regarding payment of parking fees at the airport. Some have suggested using alternative mechanisms for levying parking fees.
“The Delhi Airport may have an exit infrastructure like Delhi Railway Station, where all vehicles, irrespective of FASTag, are allowed to enter in the area and charged as per time limit at the exit,” the official said.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Why political parties are keenly watching campus polls in Odisha
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
What began as the return of student body elections in Odisha after an eight-year hiatus has turned into a larger political contest, with the state’s major parties mobilising their student wings and openly backing candidates.
With the polls offering an opportunity to influence campuses as well as gauge the mood of young voters, leaders across the political spectrum have joined the campaign, leading rallies, reaching out to students and trading charges with rivals.
A video of senior BJD MLA Arun Kumar Sahoo confronting police outside a women’s college in his Nayagarh constituency over the entry of non-students into the campus has gone viral. Ahead of the October 15 polls, BJP leader Arindam Roy also led a rally in support of students in his constituency.
The high-stakes contest has been accompanied by clashes and incidents of violence reported from campuses across the state.
The Biju Chhatra Janata Dal (BCJD), the student wing of the BJD, has traditionally been a dominant force on campuses in Odisha. But the BJP, which came to power in the state in 2024, is seeking to expand its influence through the ABVP, the RSS-affiliated student organisation. The Congress, too, has stepped up efforts through its student wing, the NSUI, to regain lost ground.
BJP-BJD war of words
The contest has also triggered a war of words between the BJP and the BJD. While the regional party has accused the ruling dispensation of using the government machinery to influence the polls, the BJP has claimed that the BJD is losing its hold on campuses after being voted out of power.
“The students’ union polls are being closely watched by all three major political parties — the BJP, BJD and Congress — which see them as an opportunity to connect with Gen Z voters, understand their concerns and cultivate support. Victories in campus elections will also be seen as a validation of a party’s appeal among young people,” a political analyst said.
Winning candidates could also emerge as political assets for their respective parties, serving as grassroots mobilisers and campaigners in future elections.
The BJD has alleged that student union elections are being cancelled in institutions where the BJP anticipates defeat.
“The BJP is fighting against Gen Z to protect its own identity. Gen Z will resist the repressive measures being pursued by the BJP. Gen Z stood with former Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik, and their support and affection for him are increasing by the day. The BJP is unable to tolerate the growing support of Gen Z for the BJD,” senior BJD leader Pritiranjan Ghadei said.
The BJD has further alleged that senior administrative and police officers are directly intervening in the elections to favour candidates backed by the ruling party.
“When nothing worked for them (the ruling party), violence was unleashed to create an atmosphere of fear among students. The message is loud and clear. Students have rejected the double-engine government and its student wing,” Ghadei added.
BJD leader Sujata Rout Karthikeyan, a bureaucrat-turned-politician, also criticised the BJP government, accusing it of allowing lawlessness, hooliganism and intimidation during the campus elections.
For the BJP, the polls carry added significance. In its 2024 Assembly election manifesto, the party had promised to resume campus elections, which the previous BJD government had discontinued in 2018.
Hitting back at the BJD, BJP leader Tejeswar Parida accused the regional party of promoting dynastic politics and stifling young leadership.
“It is ridiculous to claim that Gen Z is not with the BJP. The ABVP has won several student union elections unopposed, which proves that the BJD’s student wing has been rejected across campuses and does not even have candidates in some institutions,” Parida said.
High-voltage campaigning
Campuses across Odisha have been abuzz with electioneering, with candidates and their supporters organising lavish meals for students in college and university hostels. Posters and balloons in party colours dot campuses, while processions featuring SUVs have added to the show of strength.
The scale of campaigning appears to have far exceeded the expenditure ceiling of Rs 5,000 per candidate prescribed by the state’s Higher Education Department.
“It is no secret that candidates are being directly funded by political parties and leaders. In most colleges, the MLAs concerned, particularly those from the ruling party, are intervening in campus elections behind the scenes,” a college principal said, requesting anonymity.
Social media has emerged as another key battleground, with candidates using digital platforms to reach students, amplify their campaigns and target political opponents.
Candidates backed by the ABVP, BCJD, NSUI and Left parties, however, maintain that they have worked for student welfare over the years and are confident of making significant gains in the upcoming polls.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: Your bathroom is a hidden source of plastic pollution; here’s why
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
India’s plastic waste crisis isn’t confined to packaging, shopping bags, or discarded bottles. Some of it is integrated into one of the most routine corners of everyday life: the bathroom. Toothbrushes, razors, shampoo sachets, toiletry bottles, cotton-bud stems and personal care packaging may be used for days, weeks or just a few minutes, but many can remain in the environment far longer.
The problem isn’t just the amount of plastic used, but what happens to these products after they are thrown away. Small formats, contamination and mixed materials can make some bathroom waste difficult to collect, sort and recycle, even when the plastic itself may technically be recyclable.
DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to.
What happens to bathroom plastic after it is thrown away?
Once discarded, bathroom plastic enters the same waste-management system as other household plastic. But not all of it follows the same route.
Agni Mitra, Founder and CEO, Amwoodo Eco Products Pvt Ltd, says, “While certain plastics can enter recycling systems, low-value and multi-layered materials remain notoriously difficult to collect, segregate and process profitably. Sachets and composite packaging, in particular, often have little economic value for recyclers, increasing the likelihood of their disposal in landfills or their leakage into the environment.”
This is particularly true for bathroom products because many are small, lightweight or made from more than one material.
“The consequences extend well beyond overflowing dumpsites. As plastic degrades, rather than decomposes, it can fragment into increasingly smaller particles, contributing to the growing problem of microplastic contamination in soil and water,” he adds.
‘One lesser-known area of daily plastic pollution is the bathroom’
Plastic is part of our everyday life through hygiene-related products such as toothbrushes, razors, shampoo sachets, toiletry bottles, and personal-care packaging.
Mitra says, “A huge amount of plastic waste is produced in India each day, and bathroom usage contributes to it. What’s more troubling is that many of these products last a short period of time but linger in the environment for a much longer time.”
Mentioning data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Mitra adds, “In an assessment based on 60 major cities, it estimated India’s plastic waste generation at around 25,940 tonnes per day. The same assessment found that around 94% of plastic waste comprised thermoplastics such as PET, LDPE, HDPE and PVC, which are recyclable in principle.”
But that figure does not mean every plastic item placed in a recycling bin will actually be recycled.
So, how much of it is recyclable?
The crucial distinction is between what is technically recyclable and what is actually recycled and recovered.
“Contamination and small formats, as well as low value of the materials and multilayered construction, can make the recovery commercially difficult. This is especially important for bathroom waste products which are not intended to be circular, but convenient,” Mitra adds.
Thus, putting every plastic bathroom item into the recycling bin is not always a responsible choice. Recycling rules and collection systems vary, so dispose of products according to the system available in your area.
What can consumers do to reduce bathroom plastic waste
Reducing bathroom plastic waste doesn’t necessarily mean eliminating every plastic product. Instead, consumers can look for single-use or hard-to-recycle products they can replace with longer-lasting options.
Mitra says, “It calls for a fundamental rethink of consumption itself. Consumers can favour durable, refillable and recyclable formats, while manufacturers must accelerate the adoption of materials and designs that reduce dependence on conventional plastics.”
For consumers, simple changes may include:
Renewable alternatives such as bamboo can help reduce reliance on fossil-fuel-derived plastics for certain products.
“Bamboo offers a sustainable alternative to various everyday items, such as toothbrushes, combs, and other personal care products. It’s not about a plastic ban. It’s all about choosing the right materials for the right products at the right time and place when it’s feasible,” explains Mitra.

NEWS_TITLE_Shine_paul: SIR complaints: Panel of former judges to hold first public hearing, ECI invited
FULL_SCRAPED_TEXT:
An independent commission of former Supreme Court and High Court judges will hold its first public hearing in Delhi Thursday (October 15) on voters’ grievances over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the Lawyers Association for Constitution (LAFC) said Wednesday.
On October 2, LAFC constituted an “independent inquiry commission” in response to the “growing concerns raised by citizens regarding the design, implementation, and consequences” of the SIR, according to a press release.
The commission is headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice Madan Lokur and includes members such as another former Supreme Court judge Justice A K Patnaik, former Jammu and Kashmir High Court Chief Justice Badar Durrez Ahmed, former Delhi High Court judge Justice Rekha Sharma and former Patna High Court judge Justice Anjana Prakash.
The panel will examine the constitutional validity of the SIR exercise , the methods used, and the impact on voters. The inquiry will assess if an “eligible citizen was retained while ineligible entries were properly excluded”.
The hearing will be held at Jawahar Bhawan, New Delhi, from 9 am to 1.30 pm. The committee has invited voters who have approached it with complaints relating to the ongoing revision of electoral rolls. While Justice Madan Lokur will not be attending this hearing, other members of the Commission will conduct the hearing.
The commission has also asked the Election Commission of India (ECI) to “nominate a senior officer to attend the proceedings and listen to the range of testimonies presented by voters”. It said that the ECI’s participation will allow it to engage with the concerns being placed before the panel.
First of many hearings
Thursday’s hearing will be the first of several that the commission plans to hold across the country. Voters who have approached the panel with complaints will be able to share their experiences, which will be formally recorded as part of the inquiry.
In addition to hearing voters, the panel plans to review the electoral roll data. Its research wing will analyse additions to and deletions from the rolls, while a legal support team will examine the relevant laws, notifications and verification process.
The inquiry will be supported by multiple senior lawyers, including Kapil Sibal, Prashant Bhushan, Chander Uday Singh, Prashanto Chandra Sen, Raju Ramachandran, Rebecca Mammen John, Warisha Farasat, and Vrinda Grover.
The commission plans to complete the inquiry and make its final report public by December.
